localChanges: In Civilization II games, you can open talks with any civilization you're in contact with from the Foreign Advisor: send an emissary, then propose an alliance, peace, tribute, a withdrawal or an end to an alliance, or pick a favor (an exchange of advances, a war on another civilization, sharing maps) or a gift (gold, an advance or a unit) from its own list. Computer players also ask for an audience when they have something to say, at the start of your turn (#1007).

In Civilization II games, the Foreign Advisor and the meeting window show where you stand with each civilization (at war, no treaty, a ceasefire, peace or an alliance), how they feel about you, and their leader's title, and with an embassy their reputation (#1007).
In Civilization II games, seeing a civilization's city, as the Apollo Program shows them all, no longer counts as meeting it (closes #1067).
In Civilization II games, each trade rate stops at your government's maximum, and under Fundamentalism the window says that science gets no more than half of each city's trade (#1007).

In Civilization II games, discovering an advance that allows a new government offers a revolution to it, and a revolution in the turn you chose a government lets you choose again without Anarchy (#1007).

In Civilization II games, under the Republic or Democracy you're asked before an attack the Senate would stop, on a civilization you're not at war with, a damaged unit can be repaired in an ally's city, and you're told when a ceasefire runs out, an alliance ends, units withdraw, maps are shared, the Senate forces a treaty, a war starts and allies join it, and what the Eiffel Tower and the Manhattan Project do to reputations (#1007).
With Civilization II's art imported, New Game also offers Civilization II with three of the original's slips in diplomacy fixed, each of which the game setup can turn off (#1007).

log: makePeace ends a ceasefire, atWar counts a ceasefire as a treaty, cancelAlliance with no alliance does nothing, and DeclaredWar hears the treaty level that was broken. Given isHuman, meetingSteps' rows don't apply to a meeting a person opened.

Readers.hasSenate, MeetingRules.hasSenate and MeetingStepRules.hasSenate take the other player as well, and stance, meetingFor and the hand-over demand pass it, so a rule set's senate can weigh who it would be kept from war with. A reader that looks only at the first player answers as before.

treatyLevel answers war, contact, ceasefire, peace or alliance for a pair, and atPeace asks it. makeCeasefire, makeAlliance and cancelAlliance keep a pair at peace when only its alliance ends, and declareWar ends a ceasefire too.
declareWar takes whether the declarer was made to, and tells the DeclaredWar rules.
hasEmbassy counts an Embassy or any HasEmbassy rule answering yes.
patience and lastContact are kept per pair, written only when a rule set uses them.
shareMaps gives each player the squares the other knows. Dependencies takes an optional playerWorldRegistry.
personMeetingSteps and its pieces (audience, proposalMenu, computerAnswer, patienceEnds, spendPatienceRules) build the rows of a meeting a person opens, gated on Negotiation#initiator().

A Contact can be made from the players as well as from their units, and makeContact registers one per pair, answering the one the pair already has.
The CI workflow, scripts and tsconfig follow the current base packages, with tests.

offerGovernments now takes the revolution's key and the pending effects, and offers nothing while a revolution is under way, nor the government the player already has. registerRevolutionHandler also registers a handler that does nothing for the re-choice record, so discharging it can't throw. Tests cover the record through a save and a load, and a re-choice with no AnarchyDuration rule.

A MayRechoose(player) rule lets a player who chose a government choose again in the same turn with no interim government. chooseGovernment, given the game's rules, records the choice while a rule allows it, and revolution then makes the choice due at once. With no rule nothing is recorded and revolutions work as before.

offerGovernments is a research Complete rule's effect: for each government the discovered advance made available, it asks the GovernmentAvailable(player, government) rules, and when one says yes the engine emits player:government:available. With no rule nothing is offered.

Given the game's RuleRegistry as its last argument, the player's trade rates ask that game's MaxRate and ExcessRate rules. Without one, nothing changes. core-trade-rate is ^0.1.7.

The peace criteria treat a ceasefire as they treat a peace: acting on a player you have a ceasefire with is a sneak action, through the treaty gate, and an ordinary attack waits until the ceasefire has ended.

treatyGate's hasSenate is given the treaty partner on the target square (with cityRegistry and unitRegistry; otherwise null), the unit and the squares, as well as the player, and actionRules passes the registries it is given. A test that looks only at the player answers as before.

The atPeace criterion asks base-diplomacy's hasTreatyLevel, so an alliance counts as peace and a ceasefire does not. hasNoEmbassy asks base-diplomacy's hasEmbassy, which with a ruleRegistry also counts HasEmbassy rules; without one it answers as before.

The unit actions give base-unit-action-rules 0.1.6's treaty gate the city and unit registries, and pass the treaty partner on to SenateIntervenes as the other player: the owner of the city or units on the square, or else the player whose worked land it is. Civ1's Senate doesn't read it. treatyPartner asks base-diplomacy's hasTreatyLevel for peace. Civ1 plays as before.
Another SenateIntervenes rule can overrule a Monarchy, and replacing civ1-unit:player/senate-intervenes frees a Republic. The README says where the Senate comes from.

The Republic's and Democracy's Senate is now the rule civ1-unit:player/senate-intervenes, registered with the unit actions, and the actions that would break a treaty ask it through base-government-senate's senateIntervenes. lib/senate keeps hasSenate, which is base-government-senate's. Civ1 plays as before.

A `LeaderTitle` rule answers what a leader is called under a government, and `leaderTitle` asks for it. With no such rule a leader has no title, as before.
With no such rules, resolving takes exactly as long as it did. The README says the attitude and reputation records run the `Created` rules and are found like any other interaction.

The three records share a `RelationRecord` base, so that a reader that takes any interaction between two players as contact can skip them. `Attitude` and `Reputation` refuse a minimum above the maximum, and the README says a credit is kept unclamped and unannounced.

A handler that returns a promise is waited for, and one that throws or rejects rejects `resolve`. The README says when `Terminated` runs (before the negotiation is registered) and what happens when its handlers throw.

`Attitude` keeps how each player feels about each other, one number per direction of each pair, and `Reputation` keeps each player's reputation and the credit each other player gives them against it. Rule sets choose the ranges, and `AttitudeChanged` and `ReputationChanged` rules announce each change.
The values are saved with the rest of a game's diplomacy, and only once a rule set sets one, so games that don't use them are unchanged.
`Accepted` and `Declined` run when a proposal is accepted or declined, after its `Resolved` effects, and `Terminated` runs when a negotiation ends. They were declared but never run.
A negotiation's `initiator()` is the player who opened it, the first player it was made with, so either player can open one.
registerClasses registers core-diplomacy 0.1.9's AttitudeRecord, ReputationRecord and ReputationCreditRecord, so a game that sets attitude or reputation loads again. core-diplomacy is now ^0.1.9.
The rate just set takes any excess last, after every other rate, so a cap no longer moves the excess straight back into it. Rounding errors in the rates are left alone and don't count as a change.

When the rates an `ExcessRate` rule names are full, the rest of the excess goes to the rates it left out before staying where it was. `enforceMaxRates()` answers whether any rate actually changed. When the other rates have nothing in them, `set` now shares what's left evenly between them; it used to make them `NaN`. The README says a rule set must pass its game's rule registry to `PlayerTradeRates`.

A `MaxRate` rule gives the most a player may put into a rate, and an `ExcessRate` rule says which rates take what is over it. Setting rates keeps them within their limits and never refuses rates that come to 100; with no `MaxRate` rules, rates work exactly as before.

Re-exports the Ceasefire and Alliance declarations, and adds OfferCeasefire, ProposeAlliance, CancelAlliance, AskAlly, DemandWithdrawal, JoinWar (with the third player), ShareMaps, Gift (gold, an advance or a unit) and SellAdvance (the advance and its price).
The CI workflow, scripts and tsconfig follow the current base packages, with tests.

Computer players treat a ceasefire as a treaty, as they do a peace: they no longer pick a player they have a ceasefire or an alliance with as the enemy to march on, nor count that player's units as a threat to their cities.

Computer players no longer send their units to an ally's city, which they can't enter under Civilization II's rules. A unit steps up to an ally's city only to be repaired there, when it's damaged; Caravans, Freight, Diplomats and Spies still go in on their own missions.

When a new advance offers a computer player a revolution, it takes it if that's the government it was going to change to anyway, a turn sooner. A revolution that fails doesn't stop the advance being learned.
